questions.title: Civil Resistance — Black Consciousness and Steve Biko

subQuestions.questionText: Quote ONE piece of evidence from Source A that shows Black Consciousness was primarily a psychological liberation movement.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for ONE of the following acceptable direct quotes from Source A:
✓ 'The most potent weapon in the hands of the oppressor is the mind of the oppressed.'
✓ 'Black Consciousness is not merely a political movement. It is, above all, a psychological movement.'
✓ 'a drive toward the liberation of the black man's mind from the shackles of self-hatred'
[Award 1 mark only if the candidate paraphrases rather than quotes directly but the meaning is correct]

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to Source A. Explain the meaning of the phrase: 'The most potent weapon in the hands of the oppressor is the mind of the oppressed.'
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for an explanation that captures both ideas:
Mark 1: Apartheid's most effective tool was making black people believe they were inferior / not worthy of freedom.
Mark 2: Once a person accepts the oppressor's view of themselves, they do not resist — they are psychologically defeated before the physical struggle begins.
[Award 2 marks for full interpretation; do not award marks for simply re-quoting the phrase]

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the message of Source D (the cartoon). Use visual evidence from the source AND your own historical knowledge in your answer. (Refer to Source D in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award marks for the following (accept any reasonable combination):
Mark 1 (Visual description): Figure turning away from a distorted/broken mirror (apartheid's image) toward a clear mirror (own identity / 'Black is Beautiful').
Mark 2 (Message): BCM showed black South Africans to reject the negative self-image imposed by apartheid and to see themselves with pride and dignity.
Mark 3 (Own knowledge — symbolism): 'Black is Beautiful' slogan / SASO promoted black self-reliance / Biko argued apartheid's greatest weapon was psychological.
Mark 4 (Historical context): The BCM of the late 1960s–70s under Biko aimed at psychological liberation as the foundation of political liberation.

subQuestions.questionText: How reliable is Source B for a historian studying the South African government's response to the Black Consciousness Movement? Explain by referring to the origin, purpose and content of the source.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (ORIGIN): Source B is a South African Security Police report from 1973 — an official state document by the apartheid government.
Mark 2 (PURPOSE): Its purpose was to justify the banning and suppression of BCM — it is a surveillance document designed to paint BCM as a security threat.
Mark 3 (VALUE): It reliably shows how the apartheid government perceived and responded to BCM — useful for understanding state strategy.
Mark 4 (LIMITATION): It is biased — it deliberately misrepresents BCM's cultural and educational activities as political threats; it does not reflect BCM's actual goals.
[Award 4 marks for full coverage of origin, purpose, value and limitation]

subQuestions.questionText: What does Source C (the photograph of the Soweto Uprising) reveal about the influence of Black Consciousness on South African youth by 1976? Use the photograph AND your own knowledge in your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: The photograph shows thousands of young students marching — reveals that BCM had mobilised a generation of politically conscious youth.
Mark 2: Signs reading 'Afrikaans Must Be Abolished' — reveals that students linked language policy to cultural oppression, consistent with BCM's message of rejecting imposed inferiority.
Mark 3 (Own knowledge): By 1976, SASO and BCM had been active for 7 years; Biko had established a framework of black self-reliance that directly influenced the Soweto students.
Mark 4 (Own knowledge): The Soweto Uprising was a direct consequence of BCM's influence — students refused to submit to Afrikaans medium instruction, embodying BCM's ethos of rejecting apartheid's impositions.

subQuestions.questionText: Do Sources A and B agree about the significance of the Black Consciousness Movement? Explain by quoting evidence from BOTH sources.
subQuestions.memoText:
The sources DO NOT agree about the significance of BCM. Award marks for identifying the disagreement and providing evidence from BOTH sources.

From Source A (Biko) — Award up to 3 marks:
Mark 1: Source A presents BCM as profoundly positive and necessary — 'a drive toward the liberation of the black man's mind'.
Mark 2: Biko argues BCM is a constructive force for self-pride, dignity and self-reliance among black South Africans.
Mark 3: Biko frames BCM as the only genuine response to psychological oppression — not a threat but a form of healing.

From Source B (Security Police) — Award up to 3 marks:
Mark 4: Source B describes BCM as 'a serious threat to state security' — a fundamentally negative view.
Mark 5: The Security Police view BCM as dangerous political agitation disguised as cultural upliftment.
Mark 6: Source B calls for banning BCM leaders and publications, implying its significance is as a subversive threat, not a liberation tool.

[Both sources agree that BCM was significant and powerful — they disagree about whether this significance was positive or threatening. Accept answers that acknowledge this nuance for full marks.]

subQuestions.questionText: Using Sources A to D AND your own knowledge, write a paragraph to answer the following question: How significant was the Black Consciousness Movement in empowering black South Africans to challenge apartheid in the 1960s and 1970s?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark holistically: argument (2) + source evidence (2) + own knowledge (2) + conclusion (2).

Argument (2 marks): Clear opening stance about how significant BCM was. E.g. 'The Black Consciousness Movement was highly significant because it provided black South Africans with both psychological and practical tools to challenge apartheid…'

Source evidence (2 marks): Uses at least 2 sources — e.g. Source A (Biko on psychological liberation) + Source C (Soweto 1976 showing BCM's influence on youth) + Source B/D as supporting evidence.

Own knowledge (2 marks): Specific examples — SASO founded 1968; Black Community Programmes; BPC 1972; Biko banned 1973; Soweto Uprising 1976; Biko's death in detention 1977 and its international impact.

Conclusion (2 marks): Directly answers the question about significance — links BCM's contribution to the longer struggle against apartheid.

subQuestions.questionText: 'Black Consciousness did far more than provide psychological liberation — it offered black South Africans a complete social, cultural and political alternative to apartheid in the 1960s and 1970s.' Critically discuss this statement. Use relevant historical evidence to support your answer. (At least 400 words.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Essay Rubric:
• 18–20 (Outstanding): Exceptional argument; sophisticated evaluation; precise evidence; compelling conclusion; directly addresses all aspects of the command word.
• 14–17 (Excellent): Strong argument; good evaluation; specific evidence; clear conclusion; addresses command word throughout.
• 10–13 (Good): Clear argument with some evaluation; evidence present but occasionally general; conclusion relates to question.
• 6–9 (Moderate): Some argument but mostly narrative; limited evaluation; evidence present; conclusion weak or restates introduction.
• 1–5 (Below standard): Primarily narrative; no clear argument; little evaluation; vague or absent conclusion.

INTRODUCTION: A strong intro will agree with the statement to a large extent while acknowledging psychological liberation was BCM's most distinctive contribution.

BODY THEMES (expected evidence):

Theme 1 — Psychological Liberation (core of BCM):
• Biko's concept of 'mental liberation' before political liberation.
• Rejection of 'non-white' label — assertion of black identity and dignity.
• Black Consciousness as counter to 'colonisation of the mind'.
• SASO newsletters and Black Review promoting positive black self-image.

Theme 2 — Social and Community Programmes:
• Black Community Programmes (BCP) — healthcare, literacy, economic development.
• Zanempilo Community Health Centre, Njwaxa Leatherwork Project.
• Tangible community impact, not just ideology.

Theme 3 — Cultural Renaissance:
• Black Arts — poetry, music, theatre celebrating African identity.
• Promotion of African history, language and traditions.
• Black Theology movement — African Christianity rejecting submission theology.

Theme 4 — Political Mobilisation and Student Activism:
• SASO (1968) under Biko mobilised university students at black institutions.
• BPC (1972) — Black People's Convention as political umbrella body.
• BCM's influence on the Soweto 1976 uprising.
• BCM filled the political vacuum left by ANC/PAC banning in the 1960s.

Counter-argument (for balance): BCM remained primarily an intellectual and student movement; never developed into a mass party or armed resistance; some argue the most enduring contribution was indeed psychological.

CONCLUSION: BCM was far more than psychological liberation — it created community programmes, cultural movements and political organisations. Therefore the statement is largely accurate. Strong arguers earn 17–20; pure narrative earns 6–9.

questions.title: Coming of Democracy — Negotiations and Transition, 1990–1994

subQuestions.questionText: Quote ONE piece of evidence from Source E (Groote Schuur Minute) that shows both the government and the ANC were committed to a peaceful process of negotiations.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for ONE of the following acceptable direct quotes from Source E:
✓ 'a common commitment toward the resolution of the existing climate of violence and intimidation'
✓ 'a commitment to stability and to a peaceful process of negotiations'
✓ 'Both parties are committed to working toward lifting the state of emergency and moving toward a negotiated settlement as soon as possible.'

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to Source F (the timeline). Identify TWO specific events that threatened to derail the negotiation process between 1990 and 1994.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark each for any TWO of the following:
✓ Boipatong Massacre (June 1992) — ANC withdrew from negotiations.
✓ IFP violence / ongoing political violence undermining talks.
✓ Chris Hani assassination (April 1993) — risk of breakdown of entire process.
✓ Right-wing Afrikaner resistance / AWB / Conservative Party opposition.
[Award 2 marks for any two valid events]

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the message of Source G (Mandela's address). Use evidence from the source AND your own knowledge of the Chris Hani assassination and its significance.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (Message): At a moment of crisis (Hani's assassination), Mandela chose reconciliation over retaliation — urging all South Africans to channel grief into commitment to democracy.
Mark 2 (Source evidence): 'Now is the time for all South Africans to stand together' / 'The countdown to elections has begun. Nothing will stop us now.'
Mark 3 (Own knowledge): Chris Hani was assassinated on 10 April 1993 by right-wing extremist Janusz Walus; his death threatened to ignite mass violence.
Mark 4 (Significance): Mandela's broadcast is credited with preventing the eruption of civil war; it demonstrated that individual leadership could steer the country through its worst crises.

subQuestions.questionText: How useful is Source E (the Groote Schuur Minute) to a historian studying the negotiation process in South Africa? Explain by referring to the origin, purpose and limitations of the source.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (ORIGIN): Official joint communiqué signed by the ANC and South African government — a primary source produced at the start of formal negotiations.
Mark 2 (PURPOSE): To publicly announce the beginning of negotiations and the conditions agreed — a public commitment intended to reassure the international community and domestic audiences.
Mark 3 (VALUE): Highly useful for understanding the initial framework and goodwill of the negotiation process; shows what both parties publicly committed to.
Mark 4 (LIMITATION): As an official statement, it shows the best-case public presentation; it does not reveal the private disputes, ANC-government tensions, or the role of third-party facilitators.

subQuestions.questionText: What does Source H (the photograph of the 1994 elections) show about the significance of the first democratic elections? Use the photograph AND your own knowledge in your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Photograph shows long queues of voters, including elderly black South Africans — demonstrates the pent-up demand for democratic participation after decades of exclusion.
Mark 2: The image of elderly voters casting first-ever votes shows the democratic elections were transformative for those who had lived their entire lives under apartheid.
Mark 3 (Own knowledge): 27 April 1994 is now Freedom Day; 19.7 million people voted — 86% turnout; ANC won 62.6% of the vote.
Mark 4 (Significance): The peaceful, high-turnout election validated the entire negotiation process and demonstrated that negotiated democracy could succeed where many feared civil war was inevitable.

subQuestions.questionText: Do Sources E and G agree about the role of leadership in making the negotiation process succeed? Use evidence from BOTH sources in your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
The sources DO agree about the critical role of leadership.

Marks 1–2 (Source E): Source E shows leadership from BOTH sides — both the ANC and the government jointly committed to peace and negotiation in May 1990: 'The Government and ANC agree on a common commitment'.

Marks 3–4 (Source G): Source G shows Mandela's individual leadership at a critical moment — his broadcast prevented violence and kept negotiations alive: 'The countdown to elections has begun. Nothing will stop us now.'

Marks 5–6 (Explanation of agreement): Both sources demonstrate that without deliberate leadership decisions — De Klerk's willingness to negotiate and Mandela's willingness to prevent retaliation — democracy would not have arrived in 1994.

subQuestions.questionText: Using Sources E to H AND your own knowledge, write a paragraph to answer the following question: Why was the negotiation process toward democracy in South Africa not easy between 1990 and 1994?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark holistically: Argument (2) + Source evidence (2) + Own knowledge (2) + Conclusion (2).

The candidate should argue that negotiations were difficult because of multiple forces threatening to derail them.

Key content expected:
✓ Ongoing political violence: Boipatong Massacre June 1992; ANC withdrawal from CODESA. (Source F + own knowledge)
✓ IFP (Inkatha Freedom Party) hostility toward the ANC in KwaZulu-Natal — sporadic violence and mistrust.
✓ Right-wing Afrikaner resistance to democratic transition; AWB stormed World Trade Centre during negotiations.
✓ Chris Hani assassination (April 1993) brought South Africa to the brink — only extraordinary leadership prevented collapse. (Source G)
✓ Disagreements between parties on constitutional matters: power-sharing, sunset clauses, amnesty provisions.
✓ Conclusion must state directly why negotiations were not easy — e.g. 'Because of violence, opposition from extremists and internal disagreements, the path to democracy was constantly under threat.'

subQuestions.questionText: 'Without strong and courageous leadership from both the ANC and the National Party, the negotiation process between 1990 and 1994 would have failed.' To what extent do you agree with this statement? Use relevant historical evidence to support your answer. (At least 400 words.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Essay Rubric (18–20 Outstanding / 14–17 Excellent / 10–13 Good / 6–9 Moderate / 1–5 Below standard).

Command word: To what extent do you agree? Candidates must make a qualified judgement — strong leadership was very important, but other factors also mattered.

BODY THEMES — Expected evidence:

Theme 1 — Leadership was crucial (FOR):
• De Klerk's speech Feb 1990 — brave, unexpected decision to unban ANC and release Mandela.
• Mandela's restraint and commitment to peace despite 27 years of imprisonment.
• Groote Schuur Minute — first formal meeting; both leaders chose dialogue over confrontation.
• Mandela's television address after Hani assassination prevented civil war.

Theme 2 — Challenges that leadership overcame:
• Boipatong Massacre 1992 — ANC withdrew but negotiations resumed through Record of Understanding.
• AWB storming of World Trade Centre; right-wing resistance.
• IFP violence in KwaZulu-Natal threatened to destabilise elections.
• Internal divisions within both ANC and NP over concessions.

Theme 3 — Other factors also mattered (counter-argument for 'to what extent'):
• International pressure: UN, Commonwealth, US and EU sanctions forced NP to negotiate.
• Internal mass resistance: UDF, COSATU, civic organisations created ungovernable townships.
• Economic crisis: apartheid economy was unsustainable; business community pressured government.
• Soviet collapse removed fear of communist takeover — De Klerk's argument in Feb 1990 speech.

Theme 4 — Nature of the compromise:
• Sunset clauses — power-sharing for 5 years guaranteed NP ministers remained in government.
• Amnesty provisions (leading to TRC) allowed security forces to support transition.
• Interim Constitution — technical compromises that made elections possible.
• Constitutional Principles — binding framework agreed before Constituent Assembly.

CONCLUSION: Leadership was essential — without Mandela and De Klerk's courage, the negotiations would certainly have collapsed. However, it was a combination of leadership, mass resistance, international pressure and economic reality that ultimately produced the 1994 election. To a large — but not exclusive — extent, the statement is correct.

questions.title: End of the Cold War — Gorbachev's Reforms and South Africa

subQuestions.questionText: Quote ONE piece of evidence from Source I that shows Gorbachev believed the Soviet Union needed to change its relationship with the West.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for ONE of the following acceptable direct quotes from Source I:
✓ 'We seek not confrontation with the West but engagement.'
✓ 'The Cold War drains resources that our people urgently need.'
✓ 'every nation has the sovereign right to choose its own path' (Sinatra Doctrine quote).
subQuestions.topic: End of the Cold War — Gorbachev and South Africa

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to Source J (the economic statistics table). Identify TWO indicators that suggest the Soviet economy was in serious crisis by 1991.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark each for any TWO of:
✓ GDP Growth Rate turned negative — from +2.3% (1985) to -13.0% (1991).
✓ Inflation rate exploded — from 2.0% (1985) to 92.7% (1991).
✓ Budget deficit grew to 31% of GDP by 1991.
✓ Consumer goods shortage moved from 'Low' (1985) to 'Severe' (1991).
✓ Communist Party approval collapsed from 68% (1985) to 14% (1991).
subQuestions.topic: End of the Cold War — Gorbachev and South Africa

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the message of Source K (the domino cartoon). What does the cartoonist suggest about the impact of the fall of the Berlin Wall on the rest of the communist world? Use visual evidence AND your own knowledge.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (Visual): The Berlin Wall is shown falling, pushed by a crowd; behind it, communist regime 'dominoes' fall in sequence across Eastern Europe.
Mark 2 (Message): The fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 triggered a chain reaction of communist collapses — the cartoonist suggests this was inevitable and unstoppable.
Mark 3 (Own knowledge): The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989; within months East Germany, Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and Romania all transitioned away from communism.
Mark 4 (SA implication): The cartoon's 'SA?' label suggests the cartoonist saw South Africa as the next potential 'domino' — De Klerk's February 1990 speech confirmed this.
subQuestions.topic: End of the Cold War — Gorbachev and South Africa

subQuestions.questionText: How reliable is Source L (De Klerk's speech) for a historian studying the link between the end of the Cold War and South Africa's political changes in 1990? Refer to origin, purpose and content in your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (ORIGIN): Primary source — De Klerk's opening of Parliament speech, 2 February 1990; official government address at the pivotal moment of South Africa's transition.
Mark 2 (PURPOSE): A political speech aimed at announcing policy changes to Parliament, the media and the international community; designed to build confidence in reform.
Mark 3 (VALUE): Highly reliable for confirming that De Klerk explicitly linked Soviet collapse to South African policy changes — direct quote about 'collapse of communism in Eastern Europe'.
Mark 4 (LIMITATION): De Klerk's speech presents a carefully managed image — it does not reveal internal NP debates, pressure from the security establishment, or his private concerns about the future.
subQuestions.topic: End of the Cold War — Gorbachev and South Africa

subQuestions.questionText: What does Source J (the economic data) reveal about why Gorbachev introduced his reforms? Use the data AND your own knowledge in your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: The data shows dramatic economic deterioration: GDP falling, inflation rising sharply, budget deficit becoming catastrophic, consumer goods scarcity.
Mark 2: This explains why Gorbachev introduced perestroika — the Soviet command economy was unsustainable and failing to provide basic goods to citizens.
Mark 3 (Own knowledge): By 1985 when Gorbachev came to power, the Soviet economy had stagnated; the arms race with the USA had drained the budget; productivity was declining.
Mark 4 (Own knowledge): Glasnost was introduced alongside perestroika to allow public acknowledgement of these failures — the data confirms the scale of crisis that required such extreme openness.
subQuestions.topic: End of the Cold War — Gorbachev and South Africa

subQuestions.questionText: Do Sources I and L agree about the connection between Soviet reforms and political change? Use evidence from BOTH sources in your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
The sources DO agree about the connection between Soviet reforms and political change.

Marks 1–2 (Source I): Gorbachev explicitly abandoned the Brezhnev Doctrine — 'each country may do it their way' — confirming the USSR would no longer defend authoritarian allies globally.

Marks 3–4 (Source L): De Klerk explicitly credits the international changes — 'the collapse of communism in Eastern Europe have removed the threat that previously justified our security policies'. This directly confirms the connection.

Marks 5–6 (Explanation): Both sources confirm a cause-and-effect relationship: Gorbachev's reforms (Source I) changed the global context, which De Klerk (Source L) acknowledged as the reason SA could reform. The chain is completed by both sources together.
subQuestions.topic: End of the Cold War — Gorbachev and South Africa

subQuestions.questionText: Using Sources I to L AND your own knowledge, write a paragraph to answer the following question: To what extent did Gorbachev's policies contribute to the political changes in South Africa after 1989?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark holistically: Argument (2) + Source evidence (2) + Own knowledge (2) + Conclusion (2).

The candidate should make a qualified judgement — Gorbachev contributed significantly but SA also had internal pressures.

Key content expected:
✓ Gorbachev's Sinatra Doctrine removed Soviet support for authoritarian regimes globally — the ANC's Soviet backing changed character. (Source I)
✓ Soviet economic collapse (Source J) meant the USSR could no longer sustain Cold War competition — the global context that justified apartheid's 'anti-communist' justification evaporated.
✓ De Klerk explicitly stated the collapse of communism removed the justification for apartheid security policies. (Source L)
✓ Berlin Wall domino effect (Source K) — worldwide communist collapse gave De Klerk political cover and urgency to reform.
✓ Own knowledge: By 1989, internal resistance from UDF, COSATU and township uprisings also made apartheid unsustainable — Gorbachev was one factor among several.
✓ Conclusion must make a qualified judgement — 'to a large/moderate extent, Gorbachev's reforms contributed, but internal South African pressures were equally important.'
subQuestions.topic: End of the Cold War — Gorbachev and South Africa

subQuestions.questionText: 'Gorbachev's reforms were the primary cause of the political changes in South Africa after 1989.' Do you agree with this statement? Use relevant historical evidence to substantiate your answer. (At least 400 words.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Essay Rubric (18–20 Outstanding / 14–17 Excellent / 10–13 Good / 6–9 Moderate / 1–5 Below standard).

Command word: Do you agree? Candidates must take a stance — agree, disagree, or partially agree — and argue it with evidence. The claim is that Gorbachev was the PRIMARY cause.

BODY THEMES — Expected evidence:

Theme 1 — Evidence FOR (Gorbachev's reforms directly caused SA change):
• Sinatra Doctrine meant the ANC lost guaranteed Soviet military/financial support.
• Soviet collapse removed the 'communist threat' justification for apartheid.
• De Klerk's speech Feb 1990 explicitly cited collapse of communism as reason for reform.
• Berlin Wall domino effect created global momentum — authoritarian regimes under pressure worldwide.
• Gorbachev's economic data shows USSR could no longer sustain Cold War confrontation.

Theme 2 — Evidence AGAINST (Internal SA factors were equally or more important):
• UDF (1983) and COSATU (1985) had made townships ungovernable through mass action.
• Economic sanctions had cost the SA economy billions; foreign debt crisis of 1985.
• ANC's sustained armed struggle (Umkhonto we Sizwe) and internal resistance created instability.
• Business community (notably Gavin Relly meeting ANC in Zambia 1985) pressured NP to negotiate.
• International isolation: cultural boycott, sports boycott, diplomatic pressure.

Theme 3 — De Klerk's personal role and NP calculation:
• De Klerk came to power in 1989 believing apartheid was unsustainable on its own terms.
• He saw negotiations as the only path to protect Afrikaner interests in a democratic future.
• The NP had internal reformists who had been arguing for change since the early 1980s.
• P.W. Botha's Rubicon speech (1985) showed the limits of partial reform.

Theme 4 — Extent qualification:
• Gorbachev made global change possible; he did not directly cause SA internal change.
• But without the Cold War context shifting, De Klerk may not have had the international cover.
• A strong 'partially agree' argument: Gorbachev was a necessary but not sufficient cause.
• Most historians argue both global and internal factors were required simultaneously.

CONCLUSION: Gorbachev's reforms were highly significant — they removed the Cold War justification for apartheid and created global conditions that made De Klerk's reforms possible. However, to say Gorbachev was the PRIMARY cause overstates his role. The internal South African struggle — mass resistance, sanctions, and the ANC — was equally essential. A qualified agreement is the strongest position.
